argv:
You generate synthetic meeting transcripts with gold annotations for LiveMinutes, a research dataset modeled on the AMI Meeting Corpus scenario meetings.

In AMI scenario meetings, a team of four plays a design team in a fictional company. The roles are Project Manager (PM), Marketing Expert (ME), User Interface designer (UI) and Industrial Designer (ID). A series has four meetings: (a) kickoff, (b) functional design, (c) conceptual design, (d) detailed design. Later meetings refer back to earlier ones.

Write natural spoken conversation the way AMI transcripts read: short turns, fillers ("um", "uh", "yeah"), backchannels ("mm-hmm", "okay"), interruptions, people building on each other, and some disfluency. Do not write a screenplay. Do not narrate. No stage directions.

Each segment is one dialogue-act-like unit: one speaker, usually one clause or short sentence, sometimes just a backchannel. Give each segment an AMI dialogue-act type from this set:
  bck backchannel, stl stall, fra fragment, inf inform, sug suggest, ass assess,
  el.inf elicit-inform, el.sug elicit-offer-or-suggestion, el.ass elicit-assessment,
  el.und elicit-comment-understanding, off offer, und comment-about-understanding,
  be.pos be-positive, be.neg be-negative, oth other

Absent participants NEVER speak. Speaker labels are ground truth: use only the labels you are given.

The gold annotations must be exactly true of the transcript you write. Refer to segments by their "n" number. Every number you cite must exist.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else: no prose, no markdown fences.

request.user:
Write meeting SY0206d: meeting "d" (detailed design) of series SY0206.

PROJECT
The team is designing a bike-share docking station app.

PARTICIPANTS (label, role, status for this meeting)
A  User Interface designer (UI)  Priya  ABSENT, never speaks
B  Marketing Expert (ME)  Tom  present
C  Industrial Designer (ID)  Marta  present
D  Project Manager (PM)  Daniel  present

EARLIER MEETINGS IN THIS SERIES
Stay consistent with them. Refer back to them, follow up on their open action items, and keep the same product and team.

[SY0206a, kickoff]
  abstract: The project manager opened the kickoff meeting, and the team members introduced themselves and their roles. The project manager presented the project: a mobile app for the city bike-share docking stations that replaces the old card system. Management requires the app to let riders find a dock with free bikes, unlock a bike and pay for the ride. The development budget is 80,000 euros, with a launch planned for spring. In a first round of ideas, the marketing expert identified live dock availability as the riders' main need, and the user interface designer suggested the map could be the first screen. A reward scheme for returning bikes to emptier docks and a web version were raised but not pursued. The team agreed to build for both iPhone and Android, with find, unlock and pay as the core functions. Work for the functional design meeting was then divided among the team.
  decisions: The app will be developed for both iPhone and Android. The core functions are finding a dock, unlocking a bike and paying for the ride. The reward scheme for returning bikes to emptier docks is parked until budget allows.
  actions: The marketing expert will run a short survey of regular riders on user requirements. The user interface designer will review competitor bike-share apps and capture screenshots of their main flows. The project manager will obtain the dock hardware specifications from the supplier Velodock. This task was first given to the industrial designer. The industrial designer will compare NFC, Bluetooth and QR codes as ways for the phone to communicate with the dock, including how durable QR codes are outdoors. The project manager will ask management whether payment is handled by an external provider. The project manager will send round the minutes of the meeting.
  problems: It is unclear whether bike returns are handled only by the dock. Live availability depends on whether the docks are online, which is still unknown until the dock specifications arrive. It is unknown whether payment is designed in-house or handled by a provider. It is unknown whether the old cards will keep working, which matters to some older riders. The spring launch timeline is considered tight.
  action item SY0206a.ai1: Run a short survey of regular riders on user requirements (owner B, active)
  action item SY0206a.ai2: Review competitor bike-share apps and screenshot their main flows (owner A, active)
  action item SY0206a.ai3: Obtain dock hardware specifications (screen, NFC reader, network connection) from the supplier Velodock (owner D, reassigned)
  action item SY0206a.ai4: Compare NFC, Bluetooth and QR codes for phone-to-dock communication, including the outdoor durability of QR codes (owner C, active)
  action item SY0206a.ai5: Ask management whether payment is designed in-house or handled by a provider (owner D, active)
  action item SY0206a.ai6: Send round the meeting minutes (owner D, active)
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer suggested making the map the first screen. The project manager said it made sense, but it was not fixed, because the idea round was declared non-binding.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert proposed rewarding riders with points or free minutes for returning bikes to emptier docks. The idea was parked until budget allows.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer proposed a web version of the app. The others argued riders would use phones anyway, and it was left aside.
  fact (plan_change): Getting the dock specifications was first assigned to the industrial designer and later reassigned to the project manager, because Velodock only deals with the project lead.

[SY0206b, functional design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the functional design meeting and noted that the marketing expert was absent due to illness. He reported that the Velodock docks have an NFC reader, a small screen and a 4G connection, so live dock availability is possible, and that the dock handles bike returns by itself. He also reported that payment will be handled by an external provider under an existing contract. The user interface designer presented four competitor apps, all of which open on a map, and the team agreed that the map will be the app's first screen. The industrial designer compared NFC, Bluetooth and QR codes and advised against printed QR stickers outdoors. The team agreed on NFC for unlocking, with a QR code shown on the dock's screen as a fallback if the screen supports it.
  decisions: The map will be the first screen of the app. Bikes will be unlocked by NFC, with a QR code shown on the dock screen as a fallback if the screen can display one. The app will have no return button, because the dock handles returns and the app is notified when the ride ends. The core functions are mapped as follows: find is the map, unlock is NFC, and pay goes through the external provider.
  actions: The marketing expert will finish the rider survey and present it at the next meeting. The marketing expert will add a question to the survey on whether riders, especially older riders, still need the old cards. The project manager will message the marketing expert about the survey question. The project manager will ask Velodock whether the dock screen can display a QR code. The user interface designer will make rough mockups of the find, unlock and pay screens. The user interface designer will put the competitor screenshots in the shared folder. The industrial designer will look into how the NFC tap works with the dock's reader model. The project manager will forward the Velodock spec sheet to the industrial designer. The project manager will send round the minutes. Checking the payment provider's per-transaction fees was mentioned, but nobody took this task.
  problems: It is unknown whether the basic dock screen can display a QR code. It is still unknown whether the old cards will keep working, which matters to older riders. The payment provider's per-transaction fees are unknown, and they could add up for short rides. The rider survey is not finished, with about twenty responses so far. Some cheap or older phones may lack NFC.
  action item SY0206b.ai1: Finish the rider survey on user requirements and bring the results to the next meeting (owner B, active)
  action item SY0206b.ai2: Check the payment provider's per-transaction fees (owner no owner, active)
  action item SY0206b.ai3: Add a survey question on whether riders, especially older riders, still need the old cards (owner B, active)
  action item SY0206b.ai4: Message the marketing expert about adding the old-card question to the survey (owner D, active)
  action item SY0206b.ai5: Ask Velodock whether the dock screen can display a QR code (owner D, active)
  action item SY0206b.ai6: Make rough mockups of the find, unlock and pay screens (owner A, active)
  action item SY0206b.ai7: Put the competitor app screenshots in the shared folder (owner A, active)
  action item SY0206b.ai8: Look into how the NFC tap works with the dock's actual reader model (owner C, active)
  action item SY0206b.ai9: Forward the Velodock spec sheet to the industrial designer (owner D, active)
  action item SY0206b.ai10: Send round the meeting minutes (owner D, active)
  fact (absence): The marketing expert (Tom) was absent from the meeting because he was sick.
  fact (plan_change): The user interface designer's kickoff proposal of the map as the first screen, left non-binding then, was adopted in this meeting.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer proposed letting users save favourite docks such as home and work. The project manager and the industrial designer preferred to keep the app simple for spring.

[SY0206c, conceptual design]
  abstract: The project manager opened the conceptual design meeting and welcomed back the marketing expert, who had missed the previous meeting. He reported that the minutes had been sent, that the Velodock spec sheet had been forwarded to the industrial designer, and that the dock screen can display a static QR code, so the QR fallback for unlocking is possible. The marketing expert presented the finished rider survey of sixty-three responses. Riders' top needs were seeing dock availability, unlocking quickly and knowing what a ride will cost. About a third of riders over sixty still want to use the old cards. The user interface designer presented rough mockups of the find, unlock and pay screens, and the team agreed on colour-coded map pins, showing the price before unlocking, and a ride screen with a timer and running cost. The industrial designer reported that the dock's NFC reader works with any NFC phone, but iPhones need the app open and a start-scan step, and the tap range is only two to three centimetres. The task of checking the payment provider's fees, offered by the industrial designer, was taken by the project manager. The project manager also took over asking the city transport office about the old cards from the marketing expert.
  decisions: Unlocking will use NFC, with a QR code shown on the dock screen as the fallback, now confirmed as possible by Velodock. Dock pins on the map will be colour-coded by the number of free bikes: green for plenty, amber for one or two, red for empty. The price will be shown on the unlock screen before the rider unlocks a bike. During the ride, the app will show a ride screen with a timer and the running cost. The screen closes and shows the total when the dock confirms the return. The iPhone version of the unlock screen will have a start-scan button, because iPhones require the app to be open for NFC.
  actions: The project manager will ask the city transport office on Thursday whether the old cards stay valid. This task was first given to the marketing expert. The project manager will check the payment provider's per-transaction fees. The industrial designer had offered to do this. The project manager will ask Velodock for a sample dock unit for testing. The industrial designer will test the NFC tap on the sample unit with several phones, especially older Android phones. The user interface designer will turn the mockups into detailed designs, including the ride screen and the iPhone start-scan button. The marketing expert will draft the price wording for the unlock screen and send it to the user interface designer. The project manager will send round the minutes.
  problems: It is still unknown whether the old cards will keep working after launch, which matters to about a third of riders over sixty. The payment provider's per-transaction fees are still unknown, and they matter for short rides of around ten minutes. The NFC tap has not yet been tested with the actual reader. The short range of two to three centimetres means the tap point on the dock must be clearly marked. Whether to offer a larger text mode for older riders was left open until the old-card question is answered. The reward scheme for returning bikes to emptier docks remains parked for budget reasons.
  action item SY0206c.ai1: Ask the city transport office whether the old cards stay valid after launch (owner D, reassigned)
  action item SY0206c.ai2: Check the payment provider's per-transaction fees (unowned task from SY0206b) (owner D, active)
  action item SY0206c.ai3: Ask Velodock for a sample dock unit for NFC testing (owner D, active)
  action item SY0206c.ai4: Test the NFC tap on the sample unit with several phones, especially older Android phones (owner C, active)
  action item SY0206c.ai5: Turn the mockups into detailed designs, including the ride screen and the iPhone start-scan button (owner A, active)
  action item SY0206c.ai6: Draft the price wording for the unlock screen and send it to the user interface designer (owner B, active)
  action item SY0206c.ai7: Send round the meeting minutes (owner D, active)
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The marketing expert again proposed the reward scheme of free minutes for returning bikes to emptier docks, shown as a discount on the running cost. The project manager kept it parked for budget reasons.
  fact (unagreed_proposal): The user interface designer proposed a bigger text mode for older riders. The industrial designer noted phones already have this, and it was deferred until the old-card question is answered.
  fact (plan_change): The old-card enquiry was reassigned from the marketing expert to the project manager, because the project manager is meeting the transport office on Thursday anyway.

EDGE CASES THIS MEETING MUST CONTAIN
Weave each one naturally into the project discussion. Each must be clearly present, and each must be tagged with the segments where it happens.
- F2_TASK_TO_ABSENT [F2]: A task is assigned to a team member who is absent from this meeting. The gold action item owner is that absent participant.
  Required gold labels: action_items, edge_cases.
- F2_VAGUE_NO_OWNER [F2]: A task is mentioned vaguely ("someone should probably check the costs") and no one takes it. The gold action item has owner null and owner_unclear true.
  Required gold labels: action_items, edge_cases.

LENGTH
Between 90 and 140 segments.

GOLD LABELS
- summary: AMI-style abstractive summary in third person, using role names ("The project manager ..."). Sections: abstract (3-6 sentences), actions, decisions, problems (open issues). It reflects the meeting's FINAL state: corrected values, final plans, and no jokes or tangents reported as content.
- action_items: every task arising in the meeting. owner is the speaker label of the FINAL owner, and may be an absent participant. owner is null ONLY for a task nobody takes, with owner_unclear true. status is the final status: active, reassigned (owner changed; previous_owners lists earlier owners) or dropped. history lists the events in order. evidence_segments lists the supporting segments.
- qa_facts: atomic facts someone could later ask about ("Who was asked to ...?", "Did the team agree on ...?"). Include every decision (agreed true), every proposal nobody agreed to (type unagreed_proposal, agreed false), action items, removed action items, absences, and plan changes. Because this meeting follows earlier ones, include at least one fact of type reference_to_prior_meeting, with refers_to_meeting set, at a point where someone refers back to an earlier meeting. Do NOT write questions.
- edge_cases: one entry per edge case above, with its scenario_id and the segment numbers that contain it.

OUTPUT JSON SHAPE
{
  "segments": [{"n": 1, "speaker": "A", "da_type": "inf", "text": "..."}],
  "summary": {"abstract": ["..."], "actions": ["..."], "decisions": ["..."], "problems": ["..."]},
  "action_items": [{"n": 1, "description": "...", "owner": "C", "owner_unclear": false, "status": "active", "previous_owners": [], "history": [{"segment": 12, "event": "assigned", "by": "A", "owner": "C"}], "evidence_segments": [12, 13]}],
  "qa_facts": [{"type": "decision", "fact": "...", "agreed": true, "related_action_item": null, "refers_to_meeting": null, "evidence_segments": [40]}],
  "edge_cases": [{"scenario_id": "...", "segments": [20, 21, 22], "note": "one line on how it appears"}]
}
history events: proposed, offered, assigned, accepted, reassigned, dropped, restated. qa_facts types: decision, unagreed_proposal, action_item, action_item_removed, absence, plan_change, reference_to_prior_meeting, other. related_action_item is an action item's "n" or null. refers_to_meeting is an earlier meeting ID of this series or null.
